meta.titre: Coastal Geology and Landforms: erosion, deposition and changing sea level

sections.contenu_markdown: Cameroon's Atlantic coast has sandy beaches, mangrove-fringed estuaries such as the Wouri estuary near Douala, and rocky stretches. Waves keep reshaping these shores, removing sand in one place and building bars and spits in another, while roads, fishing villages and hotels near the shoreline are at risk. Examiners ask how coastal landforms form, what controls the speed of erosion and what landforms reveal about changes in sea level. This course gives you the processes, the landforms and a method for explanation questions.

items: Waves are made by wind blowing across open water, and larger waves carry more energy.
Rocks differ in hardness and in the number of joints and bedding planes they contain.
Weathering loosens rock and moving water carries loose pieces away.
Sea level can rise or fall, and land can rise or sink.

sections.titre: Coastal processes, landforms and sea-level change
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Processes of marine erosion
- **Hydraulic action**: waves force water and trapped air into cracks; repeated pressure widens joints and breaks the rock.
- **Abrasion (corrasion)**: waves hurl sand and pebbles against cliffs and platforms and scour them.
- **Attrition**: loose fragments strike each other and become smaller and rounder.
- **Solution (corrosion)**: seawater dissolves soluble rocks such as limestone.

### Erosional landforms
| Landform | How it forms |
|---|---|
| Wave-cut notch and cliff | Waves attack the base at high-tide level; the overhang collapses and the cliff retreats |
| Wave-cut platform | The gently sloping rock surface left in front of the retreating cliff |
| Cave, arch, stack, stump | Waves exploit joints in a headland: crack, cave, arch (cave cut through), stack (arch roof falls), stump (stack worn to a low rock) |
| Headland and bay | Differential erosion: weak rock forms bays and resistant rock stands out as headlands |

### Depositional landforms
- **Beach**: sand or shingle laid down where wave energy is low.
- **Longshore drift**: waves approach at an angle, the swash carries material up the beach obliquely and the backwash returns it down the steepest slope, so material zigzags along the coast.
- **Spit**: a ridge of sand or shingle attached to land at one end, built where the coast changes direction or at an estuary mouth. A **bar** closes a bay and may trap a **lagoon**. A **tombolo** joins an island to the mainland.

### Factors controlling the rate of erosion
Wave energy (wind strength and fetch), rock resistance, structure (joints, faults and dip), a beach that absorbs energy, weathering and mass movement on the cliff, human activity (sea walls, groynes, sand mining) and changes in sea level.

### Sea-level change
- **Submergence** (sea level rises or land sinks): rias, drowned river valleys and submerged forests.
- **Emergence** (sea level falls or land rises): raised beaches, abandoned cliffs and caves above the present shore, raised wave-cut platforms, and waterfalls where streams drop over an old cliff.
- Causes: a change in the volume of ocean water, for example by melting ice, or a local movement of the land.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to explain the formation of one or more named features.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Describe the sequence in order, naming the process at each stage and the rock property it exploits (joints, weak layers, a change in coast direction). Some papers list coastal features together with features of other agents. A **zeugen** is a ridge of resistant rock standing on softer rock, shaped in deserts where wind-blown sand abrades and undercuts the weaker layers beneath a hard cap. An **ox-bow lake** forms when a river cuts through the narrow neck of a meander in flood, takes the shorter course and deposits sediment that seals the old loop.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked which factors affect how fast a coast is eroded.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give each factor as a statement with a reason: wave energy depends on wind strength and fetch; resistant rock such as massive granite erodes slowly while weakly cemented rock is eroded quickly; many joints let hydraulic action work; a wide beach absorbs wave energy; sea walls protect one stretch but may increase erosion beyond them. One factor with its reason is one mark.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked which feature shows submergence or emergence.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Ask where the feature lies compared with the level at which it normally forms. A feature of erosion such as an arch or a stack shows wave action but not, by itself, a change of sea level. A raised beach or an old cliff well above the present shore shows emergence; a drowned valley or a submerged forest shows submergence.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain how a spit forms and why its free end is often curved towards the land. (6 marks)

etapes.justification: Explain needs a chain of cause and effect, and there are two parts: formation, then the curved end.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: (1) longshore drift and sediment supply, (2) where deposition starts, (3) growth of the ridge, (4) why the end curves.

etapes.justification: A spit is built by moving sediment, so the transport process comes first.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Waves approach the coast obliquely; the swash carries sand or shingle up the beach at an angle and the backwash returns it straight down, so grains zigzag along the shore.

etapes.justification: The question needs a reason why the sediment stops.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Where the coast turns sharply or reaches an estuary mouth, the drifting material meets deeper, sheltered water, wave energy falls and sediment is dropped.

etapes.justification: Continued supply is what makes the feature extend.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Drift keeps adding sediment, so a ridge builds out across the bay or estuary mouth, attached to land at one end.

etapes.justification: The second part of the question has its own mechanism.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Waves are refracted around the tip, and occasional waves or winds from another direction push sediment landward; the sheltered water behind the spit allows fine sediment to collect as salt marsh or mangrove.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** A spit forms by longshore drift. Waves approach the coast obliquely, so the swash carries sand or shingle up the beach at an angle and the backwash returns it straight down, moving the material along the shore. Where the coast changes direction or meets an estuary, the water is deeper and more sheltered, wave energy falls and the sediment is deposited. Continued supply builds a ridge out across the bay, joined to land at one end. The free end is curved because waves refract around the tip and occasional waves or winds from another direction push sediment landward. The sheltered water behind the spit allows fine sediment to collect as salt marsh or mangrove.

items.erreur_markdown: Hydraulic action is waves throwing stones at the cliff.
items.pourquoi_faux: That is abrasion. Hydraulic action is the force of water and compressed air in cracks.
items.correction_markdown: Write that hydraulic action is water and air forced into joints, and that abrasion is rock tools scouring the surface.

items.erreur_markdown: Longshore drift moves sand straight along the beach in the direction of the waves.
items.pourquoi_faux: The swash moves up the beach at an angle, but the backwash runs down the steepest slope. The result is a zigzag whose overall movement is along the coast.
items.correction_markdown: Describe oblique swash, perpendicular backwash and a net movement along the coast.

items.erreur_markdown: A raised beach proves that sea level has risen.
items.pourquoi_faux: A raised beach lies above the present sea level, so it shows emergence: the sea has fallen or the land has risen.
items.correction_markdown: Write that a raised beach is evidence of emergence.

items.erreur_markdown: An arch forms after the stack.
items.pourquoi_faux: The order is crack, cave, arch, stack and stump. The stack is left when the roof of an arch collapses.
items.correction_markdown: Give the stages in order and name the process at each stage.

items.erreur_markdown: Cliffs retreat only because of wave action.
items.pourquoi_faux: Weathering and mass movement loosen and bring down the rock, and waves then remove the debris and undercut the base.
items.correction_markdown: Write that waves undercut the base while weathering and mass movement help the cliff retreat.

items.enonce_markdown: Put these stages of a headland in order: stack, arch, crack along a joint, stump, cave. Name the process that mainly widens the crack.
items.solution_markdown: **Crack along a joint, cave, arch, stack, stump.** The crack is widened mainly by **hydraulic action**, with abrasion helping once rock debris is available. Award a mark for the order and a mark for the process.

items.enonce_markdown: A cliff has retreated 27 m in 45 years. A coastal road lies 18 m from the cliff edge. (a) Calculate the average rate of retreat. (b) If the rate stays constant, after how many years will the edge reach the road? (c) Give two reasons why the real rate may differ.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Rate $= \dfrac{27\ \mathrm{m}}{45\ \mathrm{years}} = $ **0.6 m per year**. (b) Time $= \dfrac{18\ \mathrm{m}}{0.6\ \mathrm{m\,year^{-1}}} = $ **30 years**. (c) Storms and larger waves can speed retreat; a sea wall or a growing beach can slow it; rockfalls and sea-level rise also change the rate. Award a mark for each correct reason.

items.enonce_markdown: Two stretches of coast face the same waves. Stretch P is massive granite with few joints and a wide sandy beach in front. Stretch Q is weakly cemented sandstone with many joints and no beach. Compare the expected rates of erosion, explain the difference, and suggest how a coastal manager could reduce erosion on Q. (8 marks)
items.solution_markdown: **Q will erode much faster than P.** Award marks for: P is resistant rock with few joints, so hydraulic action has few cracks to exploit (1); abrasion wears hard granite slowly (1); the wide beach absorbs wave energy before it reaches the rock (1). Q has weak cement, so grains are easily removed (1); many joints let water and air widen cracks (1); with no beach, waves strike the base directly (1). Management on Q: build a sea wall or rock armour and groynes, or feed sand to create a beach (1), and plant vegetation and drain the cliff top to reduce weathering and slumping (1).

items_markdown: Marine erosion works by hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution.
A headland evolves in order: crack, cave, arch, stack, stump, leaving a wave-cut platform behind the retreating cliff.
Longshore drift moves sediment in a zigzag along the coast and builds spits, bars and beaches where wave energy falls.
The rate of erosion depends on wave energy, rock resistance, structure, beach protection and human activity.
Raised beaches and abandoned cliffs show emergence; drowned valleys and submerged forests show submergence.
In an explanation question, give the stages in order and name the process at each stage.
